title: Learning at the Edge of Understanding
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick challenges the assumption that correct answers drive learning, drawing on historical examples and contemporary research to argue that correctness is a lagging indicator, not the mechanism of learning. A recent study of language models attempting to solve difficult mathematical problems demonstrates that struggling with well-structured intermediate problems—most of which elicit wrong answers—produces more learning than direct training on correct solutions. Hendrick emphasizes that what matters is the architecture of tasks, not their accuracy: even when teacher models produce only 32.8% correct answers, students learn more effectively than when exposed to 55% correct solutions in poorly structured problems. The article reframes scaffolding as a lens that makes domain structure visible rather than a ramp that simplifies tasks, and critiques AI tutoring systems that optimize for immediate success rather than learning trajectories. Hendrick concludes that good instruction aims to make success possible later, not to maximize it in the moment.
points: Correctness is a lagging indicator of learning, not its mechanism: learning often proceeds through incorrect attempts at well-structured problems.
Well-posed but flawed problems outperform correct solutions in poorly structured tasks: structure beats accuracy in driving learning.
Scaffolding functions as a lens that reveals domain architecture, not a ramp that simplifies: it enables learners to gain traction on complexity.
AI tutoring systems that optimize for immediate accuracy may harm learning trajectories at the edge of understanding.
Productive failure requires structure to be meaningful: unstructured struggle is noise, not productive difficulty.
quotes: Only 32.8% of their solutions were fully correct. And yet the “student” models still learned. As long as the problems were well-posed and conceptually relevant, they provided what the researchers call a “learnable gradient”: enough structure for the learner to gain traction. The accuracy of the answer mattered far less than the architecture of the question. There is also a telling comparison buried in the results. A separate group of teachers, trained to optimise for a different signal, actually produced more correct answers: 55% accuracy.
